query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the identity of the X element determines whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms at temperatures above 900 °C. Specifically, when X is Si or Al, the alloy forms a dense, low-growth‐stress oxide (predominantly SiO₂ and/or Al₂O₃, possibly with Cr₂O₃ admixture) that adheres well, whereas when X is Mn, the oxide formed is volatile and rapidly growing, leading to porous, cracking, and spalling scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state with homogeneous element distribution.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for extended durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at ~950 °C) in air or a corrosive environment, using alloys processed to have similar grain sizes and phase distributions, with the only variation being the X element (Si, Mn, or Al).
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and integrity of the externally formed oxide scale—either a continuous, coherent layer (SiO₂/Al₂O₃ mixed with Cr₂O₃) or a discontinuous, porous, and spalled scale (Mn-rich oxides).
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is governed by the thermodynamics and kinetics of oxide formation of the X element. Si and Al have high oxygen affinities and form slow-growing, low-diffusivity oxides that produce minimal internal stresses and adhere strongly to the alloy. In contrast, Mn forms oxides that are relatively volatile and exhibit rapid, uncontrolled growth, leading to high internal stresses, cracking, and subsequent spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Si or Al will show lower oxidation weight gains, form smooth and adherent oxide layers, and resist spallation. In contrast, alloys with X = Mn will exhibit higher weight gains, develop porous and cracked oxide scales, and display significant spallation.
generation.baseline: The CrFeCoNiMn alloy serves as the baseline, where Mn is expected to promote unstable oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-temperature exposures (≥900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, tested on CrFeCoNiX alloys prepared under similar processing conditions and microstructural states (single- or multiphase solid solutions).
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxide thickness, growth rates, and the influence of possible synergistic effects with Cr and other elements remain to be quantified; furthermore, differences between single- and multiphase substrates may modulate the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with X being Si, Mn, and Al under identical processing conditions to obtain similar microstructures. Expose all samples concurrently to an oxidative atmosphere at 950 °C for 100 hours. Periodically record mass gains and analyze the oxide scale using SEM, XRD, and adhesion tests.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity via SEM
Phase identification of the oxide via XRD
Adhesion/spallation behavior from mechanical scratch or thermal cycling tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with X = Mn develops an oxide scale that is as continuous, coherent, and protective (i.e., exhibits low weight gain and minimal spallation) as those seen in the alloys with X = Si or Al, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Question: How does the molten salt corrosion behavior of the dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy compare to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 in a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 environment at temperatures relevant to concentrating solar power systems?. System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting of high purity constituent elements (99.95 wt.% purity) with multiple re-melts for homogeneity; samples cut to 20 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm, polished to 1200-grit, degreased with acetone, and dried; corrosion tests performed in a custom tube furnace with 20 mm salt melt depth at 450 °C and 650 °C for 24 h. Test conditions: Molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt (45.4 wt.% MgCl2, 33 wt.% NaCl, 21.6 wt.% KCl) at 450 °C and 650 °C; immersion for 24 h; electrochemical measurements including OCP (1 h stabilization) and potentiodynamic polarization (-0.5 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s).
